item.title: “Monks, having heard Brahmā’s request, out of compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. With the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little…
item.description:
“Monks, having heard Brahmā’s request, out of compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. With the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties and with dull faculties, with good dispositions and with bad dispositions, some easy to teach and some hard to teach, and a few who saw the danger in rebirth to another world and the danger of faulty actions. Just as in a blue lotus pond, a red lotus pond, or a white lotus pond, some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and do not rise above the water, being nourished underwater; some are born in the water, grow in the water, and reach the water’s surface; some are born in the water, grow in the water, and rise up above the water, not wetted by the water.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta

item.title: Those who live in the world Without restraining sensual desires, Not abandoning passion, Enjoying sensual pleasures — They go to birth and aging, Again and…
item.description:
Those who live in the world
Without restraining sensual desires,
Not abandoning passion,
Enjoying sensual pleasures —
They go to birth and aging,
Again and again,
Bound by craving,
They go with the stream.
Therefore the wise,
Mindful in the world,
Do not enjoy sensual pleasures,
Do not do evil deeds.
Even if they suffer,
Abandoning sensual pleasures,
They are called those
Who go against the stream.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.5

item.title: “‘Māra, Māra,’ venerable sir, is said. What, venerable sir, is Māra?” - “Form, Rādha, is Māra. Feeling is Māra. Perception is Māra. Formations are Māra.…
item.description:
“‘Māra, Māra,’ venerable sir, is said. What, venerable sir, is Māra?” - “Form, Rādha, is Māra. Feeling is Māra. Perception is Māra. Formations are Māra. Consciousness is Māra. Seeing thus, Rādha, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … with feeling … with perception … with formations … with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, knowledge arises: ‘Liberated.’ He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.11

item.title: “Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? The eye, monks,…
item.description:
“Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? The eye, monks, is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. Forms are not yours — abandon them. Eye-consciousness is not yours — abandon it. Eye-contact is not yours — abandon it. Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — that feeling is not yours. Abandon it. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind is not yours — abandon it. Phenomena are not yours — abandon them. Mind-consciousness is not yours — abandon it. Mind-contact is not yours — abandon it. Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — that feeling is not yours. Abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.101

item.title: “Monks, I too, before my enlightenment, while still a bodhisatta, being myself subject to birth sought what is subject to birth; being subject to aging…
item.description:
“Monks, I too, before my enlightenment, while still a bodhisatta, being myself subject to birth sought what is subject to birth; being subject to aging sought what is subject to aging; being subject to sickness … subject to death … subject to sorrow … subject to defilement sought what is subject to defilement. Then, monks, I thought: ‘Why do I, being subject to birth, seek what is subject to birth? … Suppose that I, being subject to birth, having known the peril in what is subject to birth, seek the unborn, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being subject to aging … the unaging … subject to sickness … the unailing … subject to death … the deathless … subject to sorrow … the sorrowless … subject to defilement, having known the peril in defilement, seek the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna.’”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta

item.title: Standing to one side, the deity Uttara recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One: Life is swept along, Short is the lifespan…
item.description:
Standing to one side, the deity Uttara recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
Life is swept along,
Short is the lifespan —
To old age we are led,
There is no stopping place.
Seeing this danger in death,
Do meritorious deeds
That bring true happiness.

Life is swept along,
Short is the lifespan —
To old age we are led,
There is no stopping place.
Seeing this danger in death,
Seeking peace, abandon worldly hopes.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.19

item.title: “Monks, ‘bait’ is a synonym for the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Hunter’ is a synonym for Māra. ‘Hunter’s followers’ are a synonym for Māra’s…
item.description:
“Monks, ‘bait’ is a synonym for the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Hunter’ is a synonym for Māra. ‘Hunter’s followers’ are a synonym for Māra’s followers. ‘Herd of deer’ is a synonym for ascetics and brahmins. Here, monks, the first kind of ascetics and brahmins, entering and indulging, eat the bait cast by Māra and the world’s offerings. Having entered and indulged, they eat those foods, become infatuated; from infatuation, they become heedless; from heedlessness, they become subject to Māra’s will among that bait and those offerings. Thus, monks, these first ascetics and brahmins have not escaped Māra’s power.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 25 – Nivāpasutta

item.title: “And what, monks, is non-restraint? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable … enticing. If a monk delights in those forms,…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is non-restraint? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable … enticing. If a monk delights in those forms, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — then that monk, monks, should understand: ‘I have fallen away from wholesome states.’ The Tathāgata calls this ‘falling away.’ And, monks, there are sounds … odors … tastes … phenomena cognizable by the mind … If a monk delights in those phenomena, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — then that monk should understand: ‘I have fallen away from wholesome states.’ The Tathāgata calls this ‘falling away.’ Thus, monks, is non-restraint.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.98

item.title: “A boil, monks, is a synonym for this body composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished with boiled rice and…
item.description:
“A boil, monks, is a synonym for this body composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished with boiled rice and porridge, impermanent, subject to rubbing, pressing, breaking, dissolution, and destruction. It has nine wound openings, nine natural orifices. From these, whatever flows out is inevitably impure, foul-smelling, and disgusting; whatever issues out is inevitably impure, foul-smelling, and disgusting. Therefore, monks, be disenchanted with this body.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.15

item.title: “Monks, for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith, this is the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma: dwell often in disenchantment toward…
item.description:
“Monks, for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith, this is the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma: dwell often in disenchantment toward form … toward feeling … toward perception … toward formations, dwell often in disenchantment toward consciousness. One who dwells often in disenchantment toward form … toward consciousness fully understands form … feeling … perception … formations … fully understands consciousness. One who fully understands form, fully understands feeling, fully understands perception, fully understands formations, fully understands consciousness, is freed from form, freed from feeling, freed from perception, freed from formations, freed from consciousness, freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is freed from suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.146
